newsitem.title: FRANCE: AMB-Diesel jeans wins advertising prize in Cannes.
newsitem.headline: AMB-Diesel jeans wins advertising prize in Cannes.

text.p: Two television ads for Diesel jeans created by Sweden's Paradiset DDB advertising agency were awarded the advertising industry's top prize at the International Advertising Festival in Cannes this weekend.
The two ads that jointly took the Grand Prix were "5 a.m. mono village," which showed a Boy Scout troop learning mouth-to-mouth respiration, and "Little Rock," an ad set in the American West.
The six-day Advertising Festival, culminating with the awards, is the industry's major gathering for creative staff, and the Grand Prix is considered the industry's most prestigious award.
In discussing the Grand Prix winner, Bo Ronnberg, the Film jury president, told a news conference on Saturday, "We think it's a very strong concept."
"In the Diesel ads the brand has become as strong as the advertising...These are two stunningly good ads," he said.

The Diesel ads won 16 votes from the 22-member jury for the Grand Prix. The next strongest contender for the Grand Prix was an ad for Tango Blackcurrant, a soft drink, created by Britain's HHCL & Partners ad agency.
The jury awarded a total of 97 awards in the film category, including 21 Gold Lions, 25 Silver and 50 Bronze, in addition to the Grand Prix.
Britain was the top winner of Gold Lions with a total of nine, followed by the U.S. with five, Netherlands three, Argentina one, Denmark one, Spain one and Sweden one.
Of the 21 Silver Lions, the U.S. took 12, the UK four, Brazil four, France two, the Netherlands one, South Africa one and Thailand one.

In the Bronze category, the U.S. had 11, the UK seven, Brazil five, Norway three, Argentina two, Finland two, Spain two, Germany two, Thailand two, Australia two,France two,and one each for Colombia, Mexico, Denmark, Italy, Sweden, Belgium, New Zealand, South Africa, and Kyrgyzstan.
Although the jury included only two women, most jurors insisted that that was not significant in the choices made.
Tiger Savage, art director of London-based Bartle, Bogle, Hegarty and one of the two women on the jury, said the lack of greater representation reflected the number of women in the industry.
"Maybe it's because there are not as many women in advertising," she said. "This thing about women in advertising, I think it should be a sexless thing."

But another juror, Guillaume Van Der Stighelen, of Brussels-based Duval Guillaume Advertising, noted, "The jury is 99 percent men and the advertising agencies are 97 percent men, but the consumers are 90 percent women."

Roger Hatchell, president of the Festival, said the lack of more women reflected the industry. "There are probably many countires where the number of women in creative departments is low or low at the level required for the jury."
